section.title: The Altar on Mount Ebal
section.sectionRationale: In the middle of the conquest, Israel pauses to worship and to hear God's word. At Mount Ebal, exactly as Moses had commanded, Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones, offers sacrifices, writes out a copy of the law, and reads aloud all its blessings and curses before the whole assembly. It is one brief but weighty movement, the covenant renewal that grounds the conquest in worship and obedience, reminding Israel that the land is held only under the word of God.
section.thesis: Israel does not merely fight for the land; it receives the land as a covenant people, so in obedience to Moses' command they stop to worship at an altar, to write and hear the whole law with its blessings and curses, and to place themselves afresh under the God whose word alone secures their future in the land.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the altar and sacrifices on Mount Ebal with the law inscribed on stones, verses 30 to 32; and the whole assembly gathered between the mountains to hear all the blessings and curses of the law, verses 33 to 35.

units.label: The altar and the law on stones

verses.text: At that time Joshua built an {{mizbeach|altar}} on Mount Ebal to the LORD, the God of Israel,

just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the Israelites. He built it according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses: “an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used.” And on it they offered burnt offerings to the LORD, and they sacrificed peace offerings.
And there in the presence of the Israelites, Joshua inscribed on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.

units.label: The whole assembly hears the blessings and curses
units.note: not a word that Joshua failed to read

verses.text: All Israel, foreigners and citizens alike, with their elders, officers, and judges, stood on both sides of the ark of the covenant of the LORD facing the Levitical priests who carried it. Half of the people stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded earlier, to bless the people of Israel.
Afterward, Joshua read aloud all the words of the {{torah|law}}, the {{berakhah|blessings}} and the curses, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law.
There was not a word of all that Moses had commanded that Joshua failed to read before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who lived among them.

mizbeach.gloss: Altar, the place of sacrifice, literally a place of slaughtering. Built of uncut stones untouched by iron tools, the altar keeps the worship humble and God-defined, unshaped by human artistry or violence. Here Israel offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, grounding the conquest in atonement and fellowship with God rather than in military self-confidence.

torah.gloss: Law, instruction, teaching. Joshua writes a copy of the torah on stones and reads all of it aloud, exactly as Moses commanded. The land is entered and held under the torah; Israel's whole life in Canaan is to be shaped by God's revealed word, which is why the covenant is renewed by hearing every word of it.

berakhah.gloss: Blessing, the good God pronounces and gives to those who keep His covenant. Read out from Mount Gerizim alongside the curses from Mount Ebal, the berakhah sets before Israel the two ways: life and good for obedience, judgment for turning away. The covenant renewal makes plain that the land is held under blessing conditioned on faithfulness to the LORD.

basic.context: Right in the middle of the conquest, between the fall of Ai and the campaigns ahead, Israel stops to do something that has nothing to do with fighting: they worship and renew the covenant. Following instructions Moses had given long before, Joshua builds a plain altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, and they offer sacrifices. He writes out a copy of God's law on stones, and then, with the whole nation gathered between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, he reads aloud the entire law, both its blessings and its curses. Everyone is there, men, women, children, and the foreigners among them. The question underneath is: what really holds Israel's future in the land, their swords or their God's word?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative recording an act of covenant renewal commanded in Deuteronomy 27. It shows Israel deliberately grounding the conquest in worship and obedience. The specific ceremony belongs to the old covenant, but its enduring lesson is clear: God's people live under His word, and their standing is a covenant matter of blessing and curse, faithfulness and warning. The reading of the whole law to everyone underlines that all God's people are to know His word.
basic.originalLanguages: Joshua builds a plain mizbeach, an altar of uncut stones, for humble, God-defined worship. He writes and reads the whole torah, God's law, under which the land is held. And he reads aloud the berakhah, the blessing, alongside the curses, setting the two ways before the nation.
basic.typology: The altar with its burnt and peace offerings points to Christ, our sacrifice and our peace with God. The blessings and curses of the law, set before Israel, point to Christ, who bore the curse of the law so His people might receive the blessing promised to Abraham. The law written and read anticipates the word written on the heart in the new covenant.
basic.christ: The sacrifices on Ebal point to Jesus, the true burnt offering and the peace offering who reconciles us to God. The two mountains of blessing and curse frame the whole gospel: Christ took the curse of Ebal on the cross so that the blessing of Gerizim might come to all who trust Him. And the law read to all foreshadows the word of Christ dwelling richly in His people.
basic.god: God is the covenant Lord who binds His people to Himself by His word. He defines how He will be worshiped, receiving humble offerings on an unhewn altar. He sets before His people both blessing and curse, taking their obedience seriously. And He includes everyone, citizen and foreigner, in the hearing of His word, showing that all His people are to live under it.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 27 commands this very ceremony at Ebal and Gerizim. Exodus 20 requires an altar of uncut stones. Galatians 3 shows Christ bearing the curse to bring the blessing. And Deuteronomy 31 commands the public reading of the law to all Israel.
basic.oneStory: In the thick of conquest, Israel stops to worship and to place itself under God's word, remembering that the land is held only by covenant faithfulness. The altar and the blessings and curses point forward to Christ, who bore the curse of the law so that His people might inherit the blessing and live under His word written on the heart.

context.literary:
The unit is short, six verses, but it is framed with care. It opens and closes on the same note of totality: verse 33 names foreigners and citizens alike standing together, and verse 35 closes on the same pairing, women, little ones, and the foreigners who lived among them, an inclusio that brackets the whole scene and insists that no one in the camp was exempt from hearing God's word. Inside that frame the movement runs altar, sacrifice, inscription, then assembly, reading, and it tracks the order Moses had laid down in Deuteronomy 27 almost clause for clause, which is why the phrase just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded appears twice, once for the altar in verse 31 and again for the positioning of the tribes in verse 33. The double refrain turns obedience itself into the passage's structure.

Placed where it is, right after the fall of Ai and before the account of the Gibeonite deception and the great coalition wars, the scene functions as a narrative hinge. The fighting stops completely for a chapter, and nothing happens except worship, writing, and reading. A book built almost entirely of marches and battles pauses here to say that the campaign is not the main thing; the covenant is. The two mountains, Ebal for curse and Gerizim for blessing, become a kind of stage set, the ark and its priests positioned between them so that Israel stands, quite literally, inside the terms of its own covenant while the words are read. Verse 34 makes the content explicit, all the words of the law, the blessings and the curses, and verse 35 drives the completeness home with a negative, not a word that Joshua failed to read, so that the unit ends not on a summary but on an emphatic denial that anything was left out.
context.historical:
Shechem, cradled between Ebal and Gerizim, was already loaded with meaning before Joshua arrived. Abraham had built the first altar in the land there, at the Oak of Moreh, when the LORD first promised him the land, Genesis 12:6-7. Jacob later camped and dug a well nearby. For Israel to renew the covenant at exactly this site was to complete a story that had begun centuries earlier with the patriarchs, on the very ground where the promise was first spoken. The two mountains themselves form a natural amphitheater, steep slopes facing each other across a narrow valley, well suited to carry a reader's voice to a large crowd standing on either side, which is presumably why Moses chose this place for the ceremony rather than requiring it near the tabernacle.

Getting there meant marching Israel roughly twenty miles north from Gilgal, deep into hill country that had not yet been formally subdued, a detail some readers find striking given that chapter 9 opens with a coalition of kings mobilizing against Israel. Joshua 5:1 already records that the Amorite and Canaanite kings' hearts melted in fear after the Jordan crossing, which may explain how the march could be made safely at this stage of the campaign. Some manuscript traditions, including the Samaritan Pentateuch, actually locate the altar at Gerizim rather than Ebal in Deuteronomy 27:4, a variant that later hardened into the Jewish Samaritan dispute over the true place of worship, the very dispute Jesus meets head on at Jacob's well, near this same mountain, in John 4:20-21. Building the law on plastered stones, meanwhile, was not unusual; treaty texts and legal codes across the ancient Near East were regularly published on stone or plaster for public and permanent display, which is exactly the function Moses intended for the stones on Ebal.
context.canonical:
This is not the last time all Israel gathers to hear the whole law read aloud. Centuries later King Josiah stands by the pillar in the temple and reads the whole Book of the Covenant to the people, and the nation enters the covenant afresh, 2 Kings 23:1-3. Later still, after the exile, Ezra stands on a wooden platform in Jerusalem and reads the Book of the Law from daybreak to noon while the people weep and worship, Nehemiah 8:1-8. Each scene repeats the pattern set at Ebal, God's people gathered as one body to hear every word, and each one marks a hinge in Israel's story, a fresh beginning after a crisis. Joshua himself repeats the pattern once more at the end of his life, renewing the covenant again at this same Shechem and setting up a witness stone under the oak, Joshua 24:25-27.

The two ways set out at Ebal and Gerizim, blessing for obedience and curse for rebellion, run through the rest of the Old Testament as the moral logic of the whole covenant, and the New Testament does not discard it so much as resolve it. Paul quotes the curse formula from Deuteronomy 27:26 directly in Galatians 3:10, then declares that Christ redeemed His people from that very curse by becoming a curse Himself, hung on a tree, Galatians 3:13-14. What Ebal could only pronounce, the cross absorbs. And what the stones at Ebal could merely display for the eye, the new covenant writes into the heart itself, Jeremiah 31:33, so that Paul can later contrast a covenant engraved in letters on stone with one written by the Spirit on tablets of human hearts, 2 Corinthians 3:3-7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Moses had commanded this ceremony long before Israel ever crossed the Jordan, Deuteronomy 27, and the writer's insistence on exact obedience, just as Moses commanded, repeated twice, tells us what he wants the reader to notice: Joshua does not improvise. Whatever else the conquest required of him, a general capable of night marches and ambushes, Joshua submits without alteration to a script written a generation earlier by a man who never entered the land. That submission is itself the point. The narrator wants Israel, and every later reader, to see that success in battle is not the ground of Israel's security in Canaan; standing under the law, blessing and curse together, is. He also wants no one to imagine that this covenant belonged only to the fighting men or the native born. By insisting that foreigners, women, and children all heard every word, he is teaching that the whole community, without remainder, lives or dies by its relationship to God's revealed word, not by military strength or tribal status.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nothing here instructs the church to build altars of fieldstone, inscribe law on plaster, or divide a congregation between two hills to intone blessings and curses; the specific liturgical form was tied to Israel entering a specific land under a specific covenant, and it is never repeated in the New Testament in that shape. What is prescriptive is the logic behind the form. Deuteronomy itself, in the passage this scene fulfills, commands that the law be read to the whole assembly, men, women, children, and the foreigner within the gates, at set times, so no generation grows up ignorant of it, Deuteronomy 31:12-13. That principle, that the whole people of God, including those who are newest or least established, must hear the whole counsel of God and not a curated portion of it, transfers directly. So does the sober fact that blessing and curse are both real; the New Testament does not retire the category of curse, it relocates it onto Christ, Galatians 3:13, and warns that only those in Him inherit the blessing.

debates.question: Does this ceremony belong chronologically at this point in the conquest, deep in unconquered hill country?

views.label: A straightforward chronological account
views.case: The text gives no signal of dislocation and reads as a plain sequel to the fall of Ai; Joshua 5:1 already records that the kings west of the Jordan were paralyzed with fear, which would allow a rapid, undefended march north to Shechem before the coalition of chapter 9 organizes itself, so nothing in the narrative requires moving the episode elsewhere.

views.label: A topically placed unit
views.case: Some ancient manuscript traditions, including the Greek Septuagint in certain forms, place this material in a different position relative to chapter 9, which has led some interpreters to treat it as a thematic insertion, obedience to Moses set beside the sin of Achan and the fall of Ai, rather than a strict chronological report; on this view the narrator cares more about theological sequence, worship following judgment, than a precise itinerary.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage functions identically: it interrupts the war narrative to declare that covenant obedience, not territorial control, is what secures Israel's future, and the ordering itself preaches that truth whether it is calendar time or narrated time.

debates.question: How much of the law did Joshua actually inscribe on the stones at Ebal?

views.label: The blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 27 to 28
views.case: Moses' original command in Deuteronomy 27:2-8 specifies writing this law, in the immediate context of the very blessing and curse liturgy Israel then performs, so the most natural referent is that specific covenant text rather than the whole Pentateuch, a scope stone and plaster could plausibly hold.

views.label: A representative summary of the whole Torah
views.case: Joshua 8:34 says he read aloud all the words of the law, the same totalizing language used elsewhere for the whole Book of the Law, and later scenes like Josiah's and Ezra's reading of the entire law suggest the phrase intends the complete covenant document, inscribed and read in full even if abbreviated for the stones themselves.

debates.bearing: The uncertainty over scope does not soften the passage's claim; whether the stones bore a summary or a fuller text, the reading in verses 34 and 35 is emphatically total, so the ceremony's meaning, nothing of God's word was withheld, holds under either view.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the altar, law, and blessing already named, several other words sharpen the scene. In verse 32 Joshua inscribes a mishneh of the torah, a copy, but the Hebrew mishneh literally means a repetition or a second, the same word that stands behind Deuteronomy's own Hebrew title, mishneh torah, a second telling of the law given to the new generation on the plains of Moab, and behind the Greek name Deuteronomion. Joshua's stones do not merely record data; they duplicate covenant, giving Canaan its own physical copy of the very words Moses had already spoken east of the Jordan, so that the land itself now holds a witness to the covenant alongside the people who live in it.

The crowd gathered to hear it is called the qahal, the assembly or congregation, in verse 35, a term that elsewhere designates Israel specifically as a worshiping body summoned before the LORD rather than a mere crowd; the same word describes the assembly at Sinai and later Israel's convocations at the temple. That this qahal explicitly includes the ger, the foreigner or resident alien, twice named in verses 33 and 35, matters because the ger occupied a defined legal category in Israel's law, protected and obligated but not ethnically Israelite, so their inclusion here in hearing every word of the covenant anticipates a people whose boundary is defined by allegiance to the LORD rather than by blood alone.

The verb for what Joshua does with the law in verse 34 is qara, to read aloud or proclaim, the same verb used for a herald's public announcement, not a private or silent act; qara insists that the whole nation is put on notice together, in the same moment, with no one able to claim later that the word never reached them. And standing behind the English blessings and curses lie two paired Hebrew nouns, berakhah and qelalah, terms Deuteronomy 11:26-28 and 30:15-19 use to frame the whole covenant as two ways set before Israel, one leading to life and one to ruin, so that the reading at Ebal is not information but decision, calling the nation to choose.

One more detail rewards attention. Verse 31 quotes the law itself in the words no iron tool has been used, using barzel, iron, the metal of both plowshares and weapons in this period; the same restriction that keeps the altar from becoming a work of art also keeps it from becoming a monument to conquest, since iron was the material of the very swords Israel had just been using against Ai. An altar built without the tools of war stands, quite deliberately, apart from the battlefield that surrounds it on every side of this chapter.

typology.type: The altar of uncut, iron-untouched stones
typology.fulfillment: No human tool was permitted to shape the stones of this altar, so that the place of atonement owed nothing to human skill or the instruments of war. That refusal of human craft anticipates a greater refusal: the true and final sacrifice is offered not by priestly hands repeating a ritual but once, by God's own initiative in Christ, a sanctuary not made with hands, Mark 14:58 and Hebrews 9:11-12. Where Ebal's altar could be rebuilt or duplicated at another hill, and in time was, the fulfillment cannot be relocated or repeated; Christ's single offering closes the category of altar-building altogether, Hebrews 10:11-14.

typology.type: The altar built on Ebal, the mountain of the curse
typology.fulfillment: It is easy to miss that the altar of atonement stands on Ebal, the very mountain assigned to curse, not on Gerizim, the mountain of blessing, so that mercy is provided at the site of judgment before a single curse is spoken. That placement anticipates the cross, where the curse of the law and the remedy for it occupy the same ground at the same moment, Christ becoming a curse for us by hanging on a tree, Galatians 3:13. The type is imperfect because Israel's altar only prepared a place for atonement offerings that had to be repeated; the reality it points to absorbs the curse completely and does not need repeating, Galatians 3:14.

typology.type: The law inscribed on stone and read aloud to all
typology.fulfillment: Stone could display the covenant but could not obey it, and the crowd that heard every word at Ebal would go on to break much of it. The prophets promised something greater, a covenant written not on tablets of stone but on the heart itself, Jeremiah 31:33, and Paul later contrasts the two directly, a ministry engraved in letters on stone that brought death, and a ministry of the Spirit written on tablets of human hearts that gives life, 2 Corinthians 3:3-7. The escalation is total: what Ebal could only publish, the Spirit now performs, supplying the obedience the stone could only demand.

typology.type: Foreigners standing within the assembly to hear the covenant
typology.fulfillment: The ger at Ebal stood inside Israel's covenant hearing, a resident but not a native son, protected by the law yet distinct from it. That partial inclusion foreshadows a fuller one: in Christ the dividing wall comes down entirely, so that those once far off, strangers to the covenants of promise, are brought near and made fellow citizens, not merely resident aliens, Ephesians 2:11-13 and Galatians 3:28. Where Ebal could only make room within Israel's borders, the gospel makes one new people without borders at all.

study.christ:
This scene happens at Shechem, and Shechem is not neutral ground in the Bible's story. Abraham built his first altar in Canaan on this same spot, hearing the very first promise of the land, Genesis 12:6-7, so Joshua's altar completes a line running back through the patriarchs to the promise itself. Centuries later, at Jacob's well near this same mountain, Jesus tells a Samaritan woman that the true worship for which the Father is seeking will happen neither on this mountain, Gerizim, nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and in truth, John 4:20-24. Israel's whole ceremony at Ebal and Gerizim, mountain against mountain, was never meant to be the final word on where God is met; it was preparing the ground, quite literally, for the day worship would no longer be tied to any hill at all.

The two mountains frame the gospel with unusual clarity. Every Israelite standing that day stood exposed to both blessing and curse, because none had kept the whole law, and Paul later draws the exact conclusion this scene sets up, all who rely on the works of the law are under a curse, for it is written, cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law, Galatians 3:10, quoting the same Deuteronomy the stones at Ebal displayed. But the God who commanded the curse also commanded the altar, and He placed that altar on the mountain of curse itself. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree, so that in Him the blessing promised to Abraham might come to the nations, Galatians 3:13-14. What was staged in two hills at Shechem is settled at one hill outside Jerusalem.

The reading itself points forward too. A law that could be read to everyone but obeyed by no one needed a successor, not a better copy of the same stone but a new covenant written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and a ministry that gives life rather than only condemning, 2 Corinthians 3:6. And the foreigners standing that day within earshot of Israel's covenant, protected yet still outsiders, anticipate a gospel that does not merely admit outsiders to the edge of the assembly but makes them, with Israel, one new people in Christ, Ephesians 2:13-14.
study.god:
This scene shows a God who works across centuries without forgetting a single promise. What He spoke to Abraham at Shechem's oak, He fulfills at Shechem's mountains a generation after Moses, generations after Abraham, proving that His word does not expire with delay; the altar Joshua builds finishes a story God started long before Joshua was born. He is also a God who provides atonement before He pronounces sentence. The order of this chapter is not curse first, then a scramble for mercy; the altar goes up, the offerings are made, and only then are the blessings and the curses read, mercy already standing on Ebal's slope before a single word of judgment is spoken there. That sequence discloses something of His character that lists of attributes alone cannot: judgment is real in this God, but it is never the first word.

He is also strikingly patient with the means He allows for His own worship. An altar built of whatever stones lay at hand, untouched by tool, cannot have been an impressive structure, yet God receives it, because what He wants is obedience to His pattern, not architectural achievement. The same modesty appears in how He is heard: not through priestly mediation alone but through the reading of His own words, in His own terms, to everyone able to listen, so that knowledge of Him is never made the possession of a class of experts. And He binds Himself, publicly, to people who have no natural claim on Him, the ger who lived among Israel by circumstance rather than birth, showing that His covenant, even in its most nationally bounded form, was never intended to be a closed circle. The whole scene, atonement first, plain materials, universal hearing, is one long demonstration that this God's holiness and His accessibility are not in tension. Nor does He treat obedience as a private transaction between Himself and Joshua alone; He requires that the terms of the covenant be spoken where everyone, down to the smallest child, can hear them, because a God who binds a whole people to Himself owes that whole people the plain truth of what the binding requires. There is nothing hidden in the fine print of this covenant, no clause reserved for the leaders and withheld from the rest.

crossReferences.note: Abraham builds the first altar in Canaan at this same Shechem, hearing the first promise that this land would belong to his offspring. Joshua's altar at Ebal, generations later, completes rather than begins the story God started here, showing His long patience in keeping a word first spoken to one man.

Moses assigns six tribes to stand on Gerizim for blessing and six on Ebal for curse, the exact arrangement Joshua now carries out. The careful tribal division shows the ceremony was designed long in advance, down to who would stand where, not improvised on arrival.

Moses commands that the law be read to the whole assembly, including women, children, and foreigners, at set times so that no generation grows up ignorant of the covenant. Joshua's reading fulfills this pattern immediately rather than waiting for the next appointed season.

Near the end of his life Joshua renews the covenant again at this same Shechem, setting up a witness stone under the oak. The location repeats deliberately, tying his final act to this early one and to Abraham's altar centuries before.

King Josiah reads the whole Book of the Covenant to gathered Judah and renews the nation's commitment to it. The pattern set at Ebal, a whole people brought under the whole word at a moment of national reset, recurs here after centuries of decline.

After the exile, Ezra reads the Book of the Law aloud from daybreak to noon while the people stand and weep. Like the scene at Ebal, the whole community, men, women, and all who could understand, gathers as one to hear every word explained.

At a well near Gerizim, Jesus tells a Samaritan woman that true worship will no longer be tied to this mountain or to Jerusalem but offered in spirit and truth. The very geography of Joshua 8 becomes the backdrop for His announcement that God is no longer met on a hill.

Christ becomes a curse for us, hung on a tree, so that the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations. The two mountains of Ebal and Gerizim, curse and blessing, meet and are resolved at the one place of the cross.

Paul contrasts a covenant engraved in letters on stone, which brought death, with one written by the Spirit on human hearts, which gives life. The stones Joshua inscribed at Ebal are exactly the kind of covenant text Paul has in view when he describes what the new covenant surpasses.

Those once far off, strangers to the covenants of promise, are brought near through the blood of Christ. The ger who stood at the edge of Israel's assembly at Ebal, included yet distinct, anticipates a people brought fully near rather than merely tolerated.

study.oneStory:
The promise to Abraham was always a land promise tied to worship, an altar built the moment God first spoke of giving Canaan to his offspring, Genesis 12:6-7. Everything between that promise and this chapter, the sojourn in Egypt, the exodus, the wilderness, the giving of the law at Sinai, has been aimed at bringing a people back to this exact ground to receive what was promised on terms that were always covenantal, never merely military. Joshua's altar at Ebal is that arrival, the story God began with one man completed for a whole nation, and the reading of blessing and curse is the moment Israel is formally handed the choice that will determine everything that follows in Judges, Kings, and exile.

The rest of the Old Testament proves how seriously the two ways set out here were meant to be taken. Israel drifts toward the curses far more often than it walks in the blessings, and the recurring national renewals under Josiah and Ezra are attempts to drag the nation back to the very posture Joshua models here, a whole people under the whole word. Every one of those renewals eventually fails to hold, because stone, however carefully inscribed, cannot change a heart, only display expectations to it.

That failure is what the new covenant was always going to answer. Jeremiah promises law written on the heart rather than on tablets, and Christ, by absorbing the curse that hung over every hearer at Ebal that day, opens the way for the blessing promised to Abraham to reach not just Israel but every nation, exactly as first spoken at this very Shechem. The story that begins with one altar built on a promise ends with worship no longer confined to any mountain at all, offered instead in spirit and in truth by a people drawn from every nation who were once as distant from the covenant as the ger who merely stood at its edge.

quiz.q: What did Joshua build on Mount Ebal, and how?

options.text: An altar of uncut stones, untouched by iron tools, just as Moses had commanded.
options.note: Verses 30 to 31 describe the humble, God-defined altar built in obedience to the law.

options.text: A grand carved altar decorated with gold.
options.note: It was deliberately of uncut stones, plain and undecorated, not a grand carved altar.

options.text: A fortress to guard the central hill country.
options.note: He built an altar for worship, not a fortress; the pause was for covenant, not defense.

options.text: A monument boasting of Israel's victories.
options.note: It was an altar to the LORD for sacrifice, not a boastful victory monument.

quiz.q: What did Joshua read aloud to the whole assembly?

options.text: All the words of the law, both its blessings and its curses, leaving nothing out.
options.note: Verses 34 to 35 stress that he read every word, the blessings and the curses.

options.text: Only the blessings, to encourage the people after victory.
options.note: He read the blessings and the curses together; he did not read the blessings alone.

options.text: A short summary of the most important commands.
options.note: He read all the words of the law, not a summary; nothing was left out.

options.text: A record of the battles Israel had won.
options.note: He read the law of Moses, not a battle record.

quiz.q: Who was included in the assembly that heard the law?

options.text: All Israel, including women, little ones, and the foreigners living among them.
options.note: Verses 33 and 35 stress the whole assembly, citizens and foreigners alike, heard the word.

options.text: Only the priests and the fighting men.
options.note: The soldiers and leaders were there, but so were women, children, and foreigners; all heard.

options.text: Only the adult male citizens of Israel.
options.note: The text specifically includes women, little ones, and foreigners, not only male citizens.

options.text: Only Joshua and the elders in private.
options.note: The law was read before the whole assembly, not privately to the leaders.

quiz.q: Why did Israel pause the conquest to hold this ceremony?

options.text: To ground the conquest in worship and covenant, remembering the land is held only under God's word.
options.note: The obedient altar and the reading of the whole law frame the campaign as a matter of covenant faithfulness.

options.text: To rest the troops and celebrate their military skill.
options.note: It was worship and covenant renewal, not a celebration of Israel's skill or a mere rest.

options.text: Because the fighting was completely finished.
options.note: Much conquest still lay ahead; the pause was a spiritual reset in the middle of the campaign.

options.text: Because God had commanded them to stop conquering for good.
options.note: God had not ended the conquest; He had commanded this covenant ceremony through Moses.

questions: In the middle of a demanding campaign, Israel stopped to worship and hear God's word. When life is busy and pressured, how do you keep worship and Scripture central rather than crowded out?
The altar was plain and undecorated, worship on God's terms rather than human invention. Are there ways you are tempted to reshape worship around your own preferences rather than God's word?
Every word of the law was read to everyone, including children and outsiders. How seriously do you take knowing God's word yourself and passing it on to those around you?
The blessings and curses set two ways before Israel. How does taking God's word seriously, both its promises and its warnings, shape the way you live?
Christ bore the curse of Ebal so the blessing of Gerizim could come to you. How does knowing Jesus took your curse deepen your gratitude and your desire to live under His word?

translationNotes.note: The altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used quotes the law; the BSB footnote points to Exodus 20:25 and Deuteronomy 27:5.
Mount Gerizim, in front of half the people, was the mount of blessing, and Mount Ebal the mount of curses, as commanded in Deuteronomy 11 and 27.
